buffer-limits-s1.title: Four acetate buffers
buffer-limits-s1.text: Four 1.00 L buffers are made from acetic acid (pKa 4.74) and sodium acetate.

table.caption: Moles of each component in 1.00 L

buffer-limits-s2.title: Adding base to two buffers
buffer-limits-s2.text: Solid NaOH is added in portions to two 1.00 L buffers, each made from the same weak acid HA and NaA, and the pH is measured after each addition.

buffer-limits-s3.title: Three buffers of the same acid
buffer-limits-s3.html: Key: HA weak acid; A⁻ conjugate base. Spectator ions and water are not drawn.

items.q: Which buffer has the largest capacity for both added strong acid and added strong base?
options: P
Q
R
S

why.correct: Capacity for acid depends on the moles of CH₃COO⁻ and capacity for base on the moles of CH₃COOH. P has 0.50 mol of each, so it can take up to 0.50 mol of either.
options: Right: large and equal amounts of both components.
Q has the same ratio but a tenth of the amounts, so a tenth of the capacity.
R can absorb up to 0.90 mol of base but only 0.10 mol of acid.
S can absorb up to 0.90 mol of acid but only 0.10 mol of base.

items.q: What is the pH of Buffer Q after 0.010 mol HCl is added?

mistakes.why: Value: added acid lowers the acetate (0.050 → 0.040 mol) and raises the acetic acid (0.050 → 0.060 mol).

why.correct: Acetate 0.050 − 0.010 = 0.040 mol; acid 0.050 + 0.010 = 0.060 mol. pH = 4.74 + log(0.040/0.060) = 4.56, a drop of 0.18. The same acid would lower P by only 0.02.

items.q: Buffer R is much better at handling one kind of addition than the other. Which, and why?
options: Added base, because it has 0.90 mol CH₃COOH to react with OH⁻
Added acid, because its pH is below pKa
Added acid, because it has 0.90 mol CH₃COOH to react with H₃O⁺
Both equally, because a buffer resists acid and base the same

why.correct: OH⁻ is consumed by CH₃COOH, which R has plenty of. H₃O⁺ is consumed by CH₃COO⁻, which R has only 0.10 mol of, so 0.10 mol of acid would use it up.
options: Right: the large acid component handles base.
A low pH says nothing about how much acetate is left to take up added acid.
H₃O⁺ reacts with acetate, not with acetic acid.
A buffer with unequal components resists one direction much better than the other.

items.q: What is the pH of Buffer R after 0.15 mol HCl is added? (The buffer is overwhelmed: find the excess first.)

mistakes.why: Value: the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation needs both components. All 0.10 mol acetate is used up, so 0.05 mol H₃O⁺ is left free and sets the pH.
Value: 0.10 mol of the HCl was taken up by acetate; only the excess, 0.05 mol, stays as H₃O⁺.

why.correct: 0.10 mol CH₃COO⁻ reacts with 0.10 mol H₃O⁺; 0.05 mol H₃O⁺ is left over in 1.00 L. The H₃O⁺ from 1.00 M acetic acid is negligible beside 0.050 M of strong acid. pH = −log(0.050) = 1.30.

items.q: Which pairs of buffers have the same pH but different capacities? Select all that apply.
options: P and Q
R and S
P and R
Q and S

why.correct: P and Q share a 1 : 1 ratio, so both are at pH 4.74, but P holds ten times the moles and so has ten times the capacity.
options: Right: same ratio, ten times the amounts.
R (pH 3.79) and S (pH 5.69) have inverted ratios, so different pH values.
P is at 4.74 and R at 3.79.
Q is at 4.74 and S at 5.69.

items.q: Which statement does the graph support?
options: Buffer 1 has the larger capacity: its pH stays nearly flat until about 0.10 mol NaOH
Buffer 2 has the larger capacity, because its pH rises sooner
The buffers have different pKa values, because they start at different pH
The capacities are equal, because both start at pH 4.74

why.correct: Buffer 1 holds its pH until roughly 0.10 mol of base; Buffer 2 fails after about 0.02 mol. The longer flat stretch means more HA available to react with OH⁻.
options: Right: capacity is how much it can absorb before the pH shoots up.
A buffer that fails sooner has the smaller capacity.
Both start at pH 4.74, the same pKa and the same 1 : 1 ratio.
Equal starting pH means equal ratios, not equal amounts.

items.q: The pH of each buffer rises sharply once its HA is used up. How many moles of HA did Buffer 2 contain at the start? (Read where its steep rise is centered.)

mistakes.why: Value: that is Buffer 1. Buffer 2's steep rise is centered near 0.020 mol NaOH.
Value: that is the total of HA and A⁻. OH⁻ reacts only with HA, so the steep rise comes when the HA (half the total) is used up.

why.correct: OH⁻ + HA → A⁻ + H₂O. The steep rise is centered where the base added equals the HA present: about 0.020 mol for Buffer 2.

items.q: How do the compositions of the two buffers most likely differ?
options: Buffer 1 has about five times the moles of both HA and A⁻
Buffer 1 has five times as much HA but the same A⁻
Buffer 1 has a larger ratio [A⁻]/[HA]
Buffer 1 uses a stronger weak acid

why.correct: Same starting pH means the same ratio (and the same acid). Buffer 1 resists five times as much base (0.10 vs 0.02 mol), so it has five times the amounts of both.
options: Right: same ratio, five times the amounts.
More HA with the same A⁻ would make Buffer 1 start at a lower pH.
A larger ratio would start at a higher pH.
A different acid would show a different pKa, so a different starting pH.

items.q: Buffer 1 is diluted with water from 1.00 L to 2.00 L before the NaOH additions. Predict the change in each.

variables.name: Starting pH
variables.why: Dilution keeps the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] the same.

variables.name: Moles of NaOH needed to use up the HA
variables.why: Adding water does not change the moles of HA; capacity in moles is the same.

variables.name: [HA] in the buffer
variables.why: The same moles in twice the volume.

why.correct: Capacity counts moles of the buffer components; diluting the buffer leaves the moles, and the ratio, unchanged.

items.q: Which two boxes have the same pH?
options: X and Y
Y and Z
X and Z
Y and Z, which have the most HA

why.correct: X and Y both have a 1 : 1 ratio, so both are at pH = pKa.
options: Right: same ratio.
Y is 1 : 1 and Z is 5 : 1 acid to base.
X is 1 : 1, Z is 5 : 1.
Y and Z have different ratios (1 : 1 and 5 : 1), so different pH values.

items.q: Three OH⁻ ions are added to each box. Which box can no longer act as a buffer afterward?
options: X
Y
Z
Y and Z

why.correct: X has only 2 HA, so the third OH⁻ is left free and no HA remains: the buffer is exhausted.
options: Right: its acid component runs out.
Y goes to 3 HA and 9 A⁻, still a buffer.
Z goes to 7 HA and 5 A⁻, still a buffer (now closer to 1 : 1).
Both Y and Z keep both components.

items.q: Two H₃O⁺ ions are added to Box Z. Which statement is correct?
options: Its A⁻ is used up, so Z stops being a buffer
Z resists well, because it has the most HA
The pH of Z rises
Z is unchanged, because it has more acid than base

why.correct: H₃O⁺ reacts with A⁻. Z has only 2 A⁻, so two H₃O⁺ convert both, leaving 12 HA and no conjugate base.
options: Right: the base component runs out.
HA does not react with added acid; A⁻ does.
Added acid lowers the pH.
Added acid reacts with the A⁻ that Z has.

items.q: The acid has pKa 4.74. What is the pH of Box Z after three OH⁻ ions are added?

mistakes.why: Value: that is Box Z before the addition. Three OH⁻ convert three HA to A⁻: 7 HA and 5 A⁻.
Value: the ratio is inverted; base goes on top: log(5/7).

why.correct: OH⁻ + HA → A⁻ + H₂O: 10 − 3 = 7 HA, 2 + 3 = 5 A⁻. pH = 4.74 + log(5/7) = 4.74 + (-0.15) = 4.59. Particle counts work as moles because the volume cancels.

items.q: Rank these 1.00 L buffers of the same acid by their capacity for added strong base, smallest first.
options: 0.020 mol HA + 0.050 mol A⁻
0.050 mol HA + 0.020 mol A⁻
0.20 mol HA + 0.20 mol A⁻
0.50 mol HA + 0.30 mol A⁻

why.correct: Added base reacts with HA, so capacity for base follows the moles of HA: 0.020 < 0.050 < 0.20 < 0.50.

items.q: A student wants a buffer at pH 7.0 with a large capacity for both acid and base. Which plan is best?
options: 1.0 M H₂PO₄⁻ and 0.6 M HPO₄²⁻ (pKa 7.2)
0.010 M H₂PO₄⁻ and 0.006 M HPO₄²⁻ (pKa 7.2)
1.0 M NH₄⁺ and 0.006 M NH₃ (pKa 9.25)
1.0 M CH₃COOH and 180 M CH₃COO⁻ (pKa 4.74)

why.correct: pKa is close to 7.0, so the ratio is near 1 (0.6), and both components are concentrated, so the capacity is large in both directions.
options: Right: pKa near target, large amounts.
Right ratio, but a hundred times less material: a small capacity.
The pKa is far from 7.0, so NH₃ is nearly absent and there is almost no capacity for added acid.
A 180 : 1 ratio is far from 1, and 180 M is impossible to dissolve.

items.q: Why does a buffer work best within about one pH unit of its pKa?
options: Outside that range one component is less than a tenth of the other, so it is quickly used up
Outside that range the weak acid becomes strong
Outside that range Ka changes
Outside that range water reacts with the buffer

why.correct: At pH = pKa ± 1, the ratio is 10 : 1 or 1 : 10. Beyond that, the minor component is so small that a little added acid or base exhausts it.
options: Right: the minor component runs out.
The acid's strength does not change with pH.
Ka depends only on temperature.
Water is the solvent throughout; the issue is the amount of the minor component.
